title: Confidentiality, Privacy & Ownership
summary: Learn how confidentiality, privacy, ownership, attribution, and authorized use affect everyday workplace decisions.
objectives: Recognize when information or material may have use restrictions.
Identify appropriate next steps when rights or permissions are unclear.

vocab.def: A responsibility to limit access to information according to applicable rules, agreements, or workplace requirements.
Protection of personal or sensitive information from unnecessary or unauthorized access or disclosure.
The recognized authority or rights associated with information, work product, intellectual property, or other material.
Identifying the source or creator of material when required or appropriate.

sections.heading: Information can have different restrictions
sections.body: A workplace may handle public information, internal information, confidential records, personal information, customer data, intellectual property, licensed material, and other restricted content.

sections.heading: Possession does not automatically create permission
sections.body: Having a copy of a file, image, document, dataset, or idea does not necessarily mean it may be shared, published, copied, or reused freely.

sections.heading: Privacy and ownership are different questions
sections.body: Information can be privately held but not owned by the person viewing it, or owned by an organization while still containing private information. Both boundaries may need to be respected.

sections.heading: When rights are unclear, ask
sections.body: Do not guess about whether restricted information or material can be copied, published, uploaded, licensed, or shared. Use the appropriate workplace process to clarify permission.

practice.prompt: You find a useful image in an internal company folder. Does being able to open it prove that you can publish it publicly?
practice.answer: No. Public use may still depend on ownership, licensing, privacy, confidentiality, and approval.

practice.prompt: A coworker sends you confidential customer information for an authorized task. Can you forward it to a friend for advice?
practice.answer: No. The information should remain within the authorized workplace boundary.

quiz.question: What should you do when you are unsure whether material may be reused or shared?
options: Clarify the applicable permissions and workplace rules
Assume everything online is free to use
Publish it first and ask later
Remove the author's name and reuse it
quiz.answer: Clarify the applicable permissions and workplace rules

lab.objective: Classify simulated workplace information and materials by possible privacy, confidentiality, ownership, or authorization concerns.
